days.content: You can trigger an avalanche on some steep slopes that face west through north to east near and above treeline. Most of these avalanches will be small, but on a wind-loaded terrain feature, they could grow large enough to bury you. You can also trigger these avalanches from a distance, so be aware of steep slopes overhead and other parties nearby. If you experience obvious signs of instability, such as shooting cracks or collapsing in the snow as you travel across it, this is a sign that you found a dangerous area and should avoid traveling on or directly under steep slopes.

Images.caption: This avalanche was triggered by a backcountry skier around 10 feet above on the ridgeline in the Elk Mountains on Saturday November 21.
Images.altText: Looking across a snowy slope at an avalanche.

Images.caption: Shooting crack such as this image are a clear indicator that there is a slab over a weak layer and you should consider avoiding steep slopes. This shooting crack occurred near Independence Pass on Saturday, November 21.
Images.altText: A crack across a snowy slope.

days.content: It is unlikely you will trigger an avalanche due to generally low snow coverage and minimal recent snowfall. The most likely place to find an avalanche is where recent winds have drifted snow into thicker, pillow-like features. While small, avalanches in wind-drifted areas can become more hazardous if triggered above cliffs or in steep-walled creeks.

Images.caption: While this observation is not from Grand Mesa, it shows the kind of small avalanche on a wind drifted feature you may be able to trigger. Triggering an avalanche like this is unlikely and generally inconsequential unless triggered above a steep cliff. South San Juan Mountains.
Images.altText: A small avalanche with small trees nearby, blue skies, and a feature that looks impacted by wind.

Images.caption: Another place to watch for small avalanches is in loose snow on steep creek banks. This avalanche is from a different area and a different season, but is a good illustration of the kind of terrain feature that can make a small avalanche more consequential especially if surface water is present in small creeks.
Images.altText: A small shallow avalanche with willows poking through the bed surface of a steep bank and trees nearby.

days.content: Most slopes are still thin and lack a slab, so avalanche danger is LOW. You should be able to steer around isolated pockets of firmer wind-drifted snow, especially in steep terrain.

Images.caption: Small pockets of firm drifted snow could result in a small avalanche. You should be able to easily steer around these areas.
Images.altText: A jagged fracture crack cuts across a snow-covered alpine slope in the foreground, curving toward exposed dark rocks, low shrubs, and a rugged, snow-dusted ridge beneath an overcast gray sky.

Images.caption: An example of a drifted area where you could trigger a small avalanche. It wouldn't be any bigger than the area between the rocks but would be nasty if it did catch you!
Images.altText: Sunlit evergreen branches in the lower left foreground overlook a shaded, wind-rippled snow slope descending toward a dark treeline, with a sunlit, pine-dotted mountainside rising across the valley.

Images.caption: Propagating result in a snow pit on a northeast-facing above-treeline slope. It was at the bottom of the recently drifted snow in a layer of facets resting on top of a hard melt-freeze crust on the ground. Areas with this structure are very isolated.
Images.altText: A snow pit wall featuring an isolated rectangular snow column with a horizontal fracture line near its base and a vertical crack on the right, with a black graduated snow saw embedded along the left edge beneath a clear blue sky.

days.content: Avalanche conditions grow increasingly dangerous the higher in elevation you get. Near and above treeline, you can trigger dangerous avalanches on many west through north to east-facing slopes, and you can trigger them from a distance, so be aware of steep slopes above you or other parties nearby. You will probably see obvious signs of instability such as shooting cracks and collapsing in the snow as you travel to warn you that you found a dangerous slab over weak layer combination and should avoid steep, consequential slopes. Safer travel options exist below treeline, on south-facing slopes, or on slopes less than around 30 degrees steep on aspects of concern at upper elevations.

Images.caption: This avalanche was triggered from around 300 feet away on a northeast-facing slope near treeline in Yule Creek, between Marble and Crested Butte.
Images.altText: Looking across a snowy slope at an avalanche.

Images.caption: This avalanche was triggered from about 10 feet above while a skier was walking along the ridgeline. This was on a northeast-facing slope near treeline in Yule Creek, between Marble and Crested Butte.
Images.altText: Looking down at an avalanche.

Images.caption: Remotely triggered avalanches near Independence Pass from Saturday November 21
Images.altText: Looking at an avalanche.

days.content: There isn't enough snow for avalanches on most slopes. Steer around hard drifts of snow on steep terrain features and below ridgetop in the alpine.

Images.caption: Slopes in the Northern Mountains are still quite dry. As you can see in this photo of Square Top Mountain only a few gullies actually have consistent snow.
Images.altText: Fore- and mid ground slopes are snow free. The alpine slopes in the distance have a shallow coating of snow.

Images.caption: Mt. Richthofen and Mt. Mahler above Lake Agnes, near Cameron Pass. The slopes in these photos are mainly northwest-, north-, and northeast-facing. The thin snowpack on these slopes is turning into cohesionless snow.
Images.altText: Steep, alpine peaks with a thin coating of snow.

Images.caption: Surfaces in the Northern Mountains are generally very weak but there is no slab to cause an avalanche problem currently. This depth hoar was found near Guanella Pass.
Images.altText: Large feather like surface hoar.

Images.caption: This footage from Coffee Pot road in the Flat Tops shows that although they may look snowy from a distance the coverage is pretty patchy
Images.altText: A cliff-topped ridge with snowy slopes in the background transitions to forests and then ranches.

days.content: Most slopes are generally safe from avalanches due to shallow or discontinuous snow cover. You might be able to trigger a small avalanche if you find stiff, wind-drifted snow below ridgelines, on lee slopes, and around rocky outcrops in the alpine.

Images.caption: Above treeline, you could find isolated pockets of stiff, wind-drifted snow. Look for cracking in the snow surface and try to avoid pillowy or wind-buffed drifts if you find them on steep alpine slopes.
Images.altText: A pole with a crack in the snow.

Images.caption: Avalanche danger is generally safe across the region because most slopes still don't have enough snow to produce avalanches. This is looking towards Buckeye Peak and the mountains near CO-91 (Fremont Pass). There is much less snow around this area than the Mosquito Range.
Images.altText: A mountain that is mostly dry except for a little bit of snow on top.

Images.caption: Any snow that does exist across the region has been getting blasted by recent strong winds. These winds pressed snow in the alpine into thin and pockety slabs, especially below ridgelines and around rocky couloirs. This photo was taken during a strong wind event on Tuesday, November 17th near Twin Lakes.
Images.altText: Winds blowing snow over a mountain ridge.

days.content:
You can trigger an avalanche large enough to bury you from a distance, from below, or on steep, shady leeward slopes. Strong winds formed thicker and stiffer slabs below ridgelines and around convexities in the alpine, burying a layer of weak snow. The most dangerous slopes are north and northeast-facing slopes above treeline.

Avoid leeward, drifted slopes steeper than around 35 degrees to avoid triggering a dangerous avalanche. Safer travel can be found on lower-angled slopes and in wind-sheltered areas below treeline.

Images.caption: Strong winds on Tuesday, November 17th drastically changed conditions in the San Juan Mountains, finally forming a cohesive slab over our buried weak layer. The following day, numerous avalanches were triggered by backcountry travelers, mostly on north and northeast-facing terrain above treeline. Steep, leeward, shady slopes like the one pictured here continue to be our most dangerous areas. This trio of avalanches on Trico Peak was triggered on 11/18 by two skiers, and one slide momentarily caught one of them.
Images.altText: Multiples avalanches on a shady, rocky mountain face.

Images.caption: This avalanche was remotely-triggered by a skier traversing underneath the slope and perfectly illustrates our new Persistent Slab avalanche problem. Weak snow developed during a 10-day dry spell in early November and the slab that sits on top of it is getting stiffer and more connected, making remote-triggers a concern. This avalanche is small, but you trigger a large avalanche if you find a slope with deeper drifted slabs.
Images.altText: An avalanche below a rock outcropping with a ski track below it in a shady alpine bowl.

Images.caption: This shows the potential size of avalanches that you could trigger. Wind drifted snow into thick slabs on steep, leeward slopes like this one, even down near treeline. Parts of the crown here measured almost 5 feet thick.
Images.altText: An avalanche on a shady slope near treeline that runs over a roadcut.
